property_summary: For any externally-sent nonzero ETH amount to C via its receive() (from any sender), the reference contract accepts the payment and increments depositsCount (so address(c).balance increases and depositsCount increases); the mutant's receive always reverts and thus for some input (any positive amount) the mutant leaves depositsCount and balance unchanged, breaking the rule.

For any caller and any nonzero Ether amount sent to C via its receive() fallback, the reference contract always accepts the payment (receive succeeds) and increases its depositsCount; the mutant always reverts on receive (so for some nonzero amount the mutant's receive fails), violating this rule.

For any caller and any positive ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract accepts the payment and increases depositsCount (and balance), whereas the mutant revert prevents the receive from succeeding for some positive amount, leaving depositsCount unchanged and the call reverting.

For any sender and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference increments depositsCount and accepts the funds (call succeeds and address(c).balance increases), whereas the mutant that has `require(false)` in receive() will make the receive revert for some positive amount, breaking this property.

For every nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract accepts the payment (call succeeds) and increases its depositsCount (and balance); the mutant's receive always reverts, so for some nonzero amount the call fails and depositsCount does not increase.

For every successful payable call to C's receive() the reference contract increments depositsCount only when the incoming value does not cause a revert; the mutant always increments unconditionally, so there exist inputs (e.g. a failing callee that causes the receive to revert in the reference) that make depositsCount differ between reference and mutant.

For any incoming payable call to receive, C only increments depositsCount when the call does not revert; the mutant always increments unconditionally, so an adversarial callee that reverts when receiving Ether will cause depositsCount to differ (reference: no increment, mutant: increment).

For any incoming payable call to receive(), the reference contract only increments depositsCount when the call completes successfully; the mutant increments unconditionally, so there exist inputs (a sender that reverts on receiving Ether) for which the mutant increases depositsCount while the reference does not.

For any external payable send to C.receive by an EOA sender, the reference C only increments depositsCount when the call value does not overflow depositsCount arithmetic (i.e., depositsCount+1 >= depositsCount), while the mutant removes that safety check and increments unconditionally, so there exist large depositsCount inputs where the mutant overflows whereas the reference prevents the increment and thus differs.

For every payable call to C.receive, the reference only increments depositsCount when the arithmetic check (depositsCount + 1 >= depositsCount) holds (i.e., no overflow), whereas the mutant always increments; thus for some starting depositsCount values the mutant will increase when the reference will not, violating this invariant.

For any call to receive() that sends nonzero wei to the contract, depositsCount is non-decreasing (it increases by 1 in the reference); the mutant that decrements depositsCount can make depositsCount decrease for some input value/actor.

For any incoming payable call to receive (from any sender with any nonzero amount), the contract's depositsCount never decreases (it is non-decreasing); the mutant that decrements in receive can make depositsCount decrease for some inputs.

For any payable incoming call to receive, depositsCount never becomes less than its previous value (i.e., receive is non-decreasing); the mutant that decrements depositsCount can make the count decrease for some input sender/amount.

For any single payable call to receive() (from any caller, any nonzero value), the depositsCount after the call equals its previous value plus 1 (i.e., depositsCount increments by exactly 1); the mutant that decrements breaks this since some call leads to depositsCount == previous - 1.

For every payable incoming call to receive, the contract's depositsCount never decreases (i.e., depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements depositsCount in receive can make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some fuzzed sender/amount.

For any non-negative ether transfer to C via its receive entry, the reference contract always increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount increases by exactly 1 after any receive call that sends any amount, including zero), whereas the mutant fails by not incrementing when msg.value == 0; thus there exists an input (msg.value == 0) that breaks the rule.
For every call to C's receive (from any sender/amount), depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant fails this when msg.value == 0 because it conditionally skips the increment.

For every payable call to receive(), depositsCount never decreases (i.e., depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant using unchecked++ can wrap on overflow and make depositsCount decrease, violating this rule for some input.

For any single payable call to receive, the contract's depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); replacing the checked increment with unchecked can overflow and make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some input.

For any single payable call to receive() from any sender with any value, the reference contract's depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant uses unchecked++ which can overflow and make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some initial depositsCount and input.

For any single payable call to receive(), the reference contract's depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before) because increments are checked; the mutant uses unchecked++ so on overflow depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some inputs.

For any initial depositsCount and any single payable call to receive, the checked contract guarantees depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1 (i.e. increments by exactly one without wrapping), whereas the mutant using unchecked++ can overflow and make depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1 for some initial depositsCount.
Only the contract owner can cause the contract to decrease its own balance via withdrawAll (i.e., withdrawAll cannot reduce address(c).balance when called by a non-owner).
Only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll (i.e., non-owners' calls revert).
A caller that is not the owner must observe a revert when calling c.withdrawAll().
A caller different from the contract owner must observe a revert when calling c.withdrawAll().
A caller that is not the owner must observe a revert when calling c.withdrawAll().

For any caller and any value sent through sendMoney(target, value) from the owner, the reference contract C preserves its own balance such that calling withdrawAll afterwards still lets the owner withdraw the full contract balance (i.e., onlyOwner prevents outsiders from draining funds via withdrawAll), whereas the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows a non-owner caller to call withdrawAll and reduce/empty the contract balance, violating that preservation.

For any caller and any target+amount, if the contract C's owner sends money out via sendMoney(target, amount) to an external counterparty that re-enters by calling withdrawAll, the original contract preserves that only the owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance afterwards; the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows the adversarial target to call withdrawAll and reduce address(c).balance, violating that preservation for some inputs.

For any adversarial callee and any sent amount, calling c.sendMoney(target, amount) as the owner cannot result in the contract balance decreasing due to an external reentrant call to withdrawAll because only the owner can call withdrawAll in the correct contract; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows the adversarial callee to re-enter and drain the contract, violating that the contract balance remains equal to the pre-send balance minus the sent amount only when the callee does not gain additional withdrawal privileges.

For all targets and amounts sent via sendMoney by the owner, after that send completes the contract's balance equals its previous balance minus the sent amount (i.e., no outsider can additionally trigger withdrawAll during the external call to further drain funds); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows the callee (if it reenters) to call withdrawAll and further reduce the contract balance, violating this property for some inputs.

For every target address T and send amount A (sent by the owner), after c.sendMoney(T,A) completes the contract's balance equals its prior balance minus A (i.e., no extra funds were drained during the external call); the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows an attacker contract T to additionally call withdrawAll during the external call and further reduce address(c).balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any recipient whose fallback/receive may revert, the reference contract's withdrawAll (which calls internal withdraw) preserves that a withdrawAll call DOES NOT revert because the internal withdraw uses transfer to msg.sender and thus will revert if recipient's fallback reverts; the mutant that replaces the internal call with a direct transfer to owner changes who receives funds and can make the call succeed/fail differently — specifically, when the owner is a contract whose receive() reverts, the mutant transfers directly to owner (causing revert) whereas the reference routes through withdraw which sends to msg.sender (the caller) and may behave differently, so the observable behavior (success/failure and balances) can differ.

For any caller who is the owner, calling withdrawAll forwards the contract balance to the caller (msg.sender) via the internal withdraw call in the reference, so withdrawAll succeeds and leaves the contract balance zero and the caller's balance increased accordingly; the mutant that transfers directly to owner can behave differently when the owner is a contract whose receive() reverts, causing different success/failure or balances for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any payable balance in the contract, calling withdrawAll always results in the contract balance becoming zero and the caller (msg.sender) receiving those funds (reference); the mutant that sends funds to owner directly can leave the contract balance non-zero or revert when owner is a contract with a reverting receive, so this property is violated for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll on the reference always forwards the contract's balance to msg.sender (the caller) and succeeds (leaving address(c).balance == 0 and increasing caller balance), whereas the mutant sends directly to owner (stored address) so when owner != msg.sender and owner is a reverting contract the mutant can revert or leave funds trapped — thus the general rule: withdrawAll called by owner always succeeds and empties contract balance by crediting msg.sender; the mutant breaks this for some owner contracts.

For any caller who is the current owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll returns successfully (does not revert) on the reference C because it ultimately calls withdraw which sends funds to msg.sender; the mutant that transfers directly to stored owner can revert for some inputs where owner is a contract with a reverting receive(), so the property is: withdrawAll called by owner never reverts (reference: always true), but the mutant can cause withdrawAll to revert for some owner contract addresses.

After any owner-funded deposit, calling withdrawAll always reduces the contract balance to zero in the reference implementation; the mutant that calls withdraw(0) leaves a non-zero balance for some inputs and thus violates this rule.

For any depositor and deposit amount > 0, after depositing to C and then calling withdrawAll as the owner, the contract balance becomes zero in the reference but the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a non-zero balance (so withdrawAll always empties the contract in the correct contract, but not in the buggy one).

For any positive deposit amount and any depositor, if the owner calls withdrawAll after funds exist in the contract then the contract balance becomes zero (the mutant that calls withdraw(0) leaves a non-zero balance for some deposits).

For any deposit amount and depositor where the contract has non-zero balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll the contract balance becomes zero in the reference implementation; the mutant calling withdraw(0) can leave a non-zero contract balance, so the property is that withdrawAll always empties the contract balance.

For any nonzero amount deposited to the contract by any depositor, when the owner calls withdrawAll the contract's balance becomes zero (the buggy mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a non-zero balance), so the reference always empties the contract while the mutant does not for some deposits.

For any caller who is the owner and for any amount up to the contract balance, the reference contract always reverts on failed sends to the owner (so withdraw either succeeds and reduces contract balance or reverts); the mutant using call can silently fail to transfer funds (leaving contract balance unchanged) so there exist inputs where behavior differs.

For any caller that is owner and any withdraw amount up to the contract balance, the reference contract always transfers the funds (reducing address(c).balance by that amount) or reverts; the mutant that uses call may return successfully while leaving contract balance unchanged when the recipient reverts, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any owner-triggered withdraw of amount x (with owner being the deployer), the reference contract either transfers x out (reducing address(c).balance by x) or reverts; the mutant that uses call may silently fail to send funds to a reverting recipient leaving address(c).balance unchanged, so there exist inputs (amount and a reverting recipient) where the mutant violates this balance-change rule.

For any owner-initiated withdraw(amount) when the recipient address's fallback/receive reverts, the reference (which uses transfer) will revert the withdraw call (so the call does not succeed), whereas the mutant (which uses call and ignores the success flag) may return successfully even though funds were not sent; the test asserts that withdraw reverts for a reverting recipient.

For any caller that is owner and any withdraw amount, the reference contract always either succeeds in transferring the requested amount to the recipient or reverts; specifically, when the recipient's fallback/receive consumes all gas (e.g., an infinite loop via gas exhaustion), transfer will still revert (thus withdraw reverts) while the mutant's unchecked call may return (silently failing to move funds) — so the invariant is that withdraw either reverts or reduces address(c).balance by the requested amount, which the mutant can violate for some fuzzed amount and a gas-consuming recipient.
Calling sendMoney with an amount that would make the target revert must NOT revert the call (i.e., sendMoney never reverts on transfer failure), so a boolean success check is not required.
